\section[el flechazo]{el flechazo — love at first sight}

\label{lesson:ES-C744-flechazo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for well-being, then the Spanish for self-esteem.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el flechazo}
\textbf{el flechazo} — \textquotedblleft{}love at first sight\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Fue un flechazo: nos casamos en un año.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It was love at first sight: we married within a year.}
\end{quote}

Literally an arrow shot, Cupid's arrow.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{flechazo} is built on \emph{flecha} \textquotedblleft{}arrow\textquotedblright{} with \emph{-azo}, the ending for a blow. \emph{Flecha} is usually traced to French \emph{flèche}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el flechazo}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el flechazo}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for well-being, then the Spanish for self-esteem, then say \emph{el flechazo} again
\end{itemize}

\section[el piropo]{el piropo — the compliment (flirtatious)}

\label{lesson:ES-C744-piropo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for self-esteem, then the Spanish for love at first sight.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el piropo}
\textbf{el piropo} — \textquotedblleft{}the compliment (flirtatious)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mi marido siempre me echa piropos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My husband is always paying me compliments.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Echar un piropo} — to pay someone a flirtatious compliment. From a stranger in the street, a \emph{piropo} is now widely seen as harassment.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{piropo} comes from Latin \emph{pyrōpus} \textquotedblleft{}gold-bronze\textquotedblright{}, from Greek \emph{pyrōpós} \textquotedblleft{}fire-coloured\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short); the name of a red gem became the word for a sparkling compliment.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el piropo}, once more

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for self-esteem, then the Spanish for love at first sight, then say \emph{el piropo} again
\end{itemize}

\section[el noviazgo]{el noviazgo — the courtship, the engagement}

\label{lesson:ES-C744-noviazgo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for love at first sight, then the Spanish for the compliment.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el noviazgo}
\textbf{el noviazgo} — \textquotedblleft{}the courtship, the engagement\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tuvieron un noviazgo de cinco años.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Their courtship lasted five years.}
\end{quote}

The time when two people are \emph{novios}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{noviazgo} is built on \emph{novio} with the ending \emph{-azgo}; \emph{novio} comes from a spoken Latin \emph{novius} \textquotedblleft{}newly married\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{novus} \textquotedblleft{}new\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB, under \emph{novio}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[el pretendiente]{el pretendiente — the suitor, the admirer}

\label{lesson:ES-C744-pretendiente}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the compliment, then the Spanish for the courtship.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el pretendiente}
\textbf{el pretendiente} — \textquotedblleft{}the suitor, the admirer\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tiene muchos pretendientes.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She has a lot of admirers.}
\end{quote}

Also a candidate for a job or a throne.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{pretendiente} is built on \emph{pretender} \textquotedblleft{}to aim at, to court\textquotedblright{}, a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{praetendere} \textquotedblleft{}to hold out in front\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{tendere} \textquotedblleft{}to stretch\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la complicidad]{la complicidad — closeness, understanding; complicity}

\label{lesson:ES-C744-complicidad}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the courtship, then the Spanish for the suitor.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la complicidad}
\textbf{la complicidad} — \textquotedblleft{}closeness, understanding; complicity\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Entre ellos hay mucha complicidad.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There is a great understanding between them.}
\end{quote}

Between friends or partners it is a warm word; in law it is complicity.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{complicidad} is built on \emph{cómplice}, usually described as a learned borrowing from Late Latin \emph{complex}, \emph{complicem} \textquotedblleft{}closely joined\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{plicāre} \textquotedblleft{}to fold\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
